phrases.explanation: The opening places the recitation under Allah's name, seeking blessing and help from Him. The commentary connects this invocation with the beginning of the Qur'an and with the practice of starting important acts in God's name. It also discusses whether this verse belongs to the opening chapter as its first verse. The wording here is retained as part of the received text without making that broader question a condition of its meaning.

The invocation names Allah and then moves directly to two descriptions of His mercy. Naming Him at the start asks for blessing and help, while the titles that follow shape how the worshipper understands the One invoked. The commentary discusses whether the opening formula is counted as a verse. That question concerns verse numbering, not the sense of these names.

This name describes Allah's vast mercy, which reaches creation broadly. The commentary notes that the form of the name conveys an expansive quality of mercy, rather than a kindness limited to a particular person or moment. In the opening, it gives the invocation a tone of hope: the One whose name is invoked is not merely powerful, but characterized by encompassing compassion.

This closely related name emphasizes mercy as well, with the commentary distinguishing it as especially associated with sustained or particular mercy. The two names together therefore do more than repeat one idea: they present mercy in its breadth and its continuing care. Their placement at the start of the chapter frames the relationship between God and those who worship Him through compassion.

The declaration gathers every true form of praise, rather than reserving praise for one blessing or one moment. The commentary explains that praise belongs to Allah because He is the source of creation and goodness, and because His qualities merit it in themselves. The opening thus directs gratitude beyond a particular favor toward the One worthy of praise in every circumstance.

Praise is directed to Allah alone as its ultimate recipient. The wording is not simply a report that people happen to praise Him. It establishes where all praise properly belongs. The commentary links this to God's perfection and beneficence. Human beings may praise one another for good actions, but the source and fullest ground of every good ultimately return to Allah.

Allah is the Lord who creates, sustains, and governs every realm of created beings. The commentary discusses the meaning of the worlds as the many kinds or communities of creation, not only the human world. Calling Him their Lord grounds the praise just declared: all existence depends on His care and authority, and no part of creation falls outside His governance.

The verse returns to the name expressing Allah's encompassing mercy. The commentary treats this repetition as meaningful: after describing Him as Lord of all worlds, it foregrounds compassion as a defining quality of His relation to creation. His lordship is not presented as bare control, but as care and mercy extending across the beings He sustains.

The second name again points to mercy, with an emphasis the commentary distinguishes from the preceding name: mercy that is ongoing and especially bestowed. Together, the names balance breadth with particular care. Their repetition after the description of Allah's lordship keeps the worshipper's understanding of divine authority joined to mercy, rather than allowing power to be imagined apart from compassion.

The title affirms Allah's complete authority and ownership. The commentary explains the expression through the idea of a sovereign whose command cannot be overridden, while also noting the related sense of one who possesses and governs. Here that authority is attached specifically to the final Day, when worldly claims to power no longer offer protection or control.

This is the day when creation is raised and judged, and each person faces the outcome of their deeds. The commentary describes it as the Day of Recompense, when Allah alone determines reward and punishment with justice. The phrase makes accountability central to the chapter's portrait of God: the merciful Lord is also the sovereign judge before whom every life is answerable.

The worshipper addresses Allah directly and reserves worship for Him alone. The commentary understands this as a declaration of exclusive devotion: no created being shares God's right to be worshipped. The direct address also changes the chapter from describing Allah to speaking to Him, making the words a personal act of faith rather than only a statement about belief.

Worship includes submission, obedience, and acts of devotion offered to Allah. The commentary discusses the range of meanings carried by the Arabic term, so the statement is broader than performing a single ritual. The plural “we” places the speaker among a community of worshippers, expressing shared dependence while affirming that their devotion is directed to Allah.

The repeated emphasis on Allah alone marks a second exclusive commitment. The verse does not limit God's uniqueness to worship. It also makes Him the sole source from whom help is ultimately sought. The commentary treats the repetition as purposeful, distinguishing devotion from reliance while joining both in the worshipper's relationship with Allah.

The worshippers acknowledge that they cannot fulfill their duties or meet their needs without Allah's support. The commentary connects this request to seeking aid in obedience and worship, while the wording can encompass other needs as well. By asking collectively, the verse expresses humility and dependence, not passivity: people act and worship, but recognize that success and strength come from God.

The request asks Allah to show the worshippers the way and help them remain upon it. The commentary explains guidance as more than simply making a path known: it includes directing people toward truth and granting them the ability to follow it. The plural request is ongoing, expressing a need for divine direction throughout life rather than a single moment of instruction.

The path is the clear way of faith and obedience that leads to Allah's approval. The commentary identifies it with Islam and with following God's commands, while describing it as a way free from deviation. The image joins direction with conduct: the worshipper seeks not only correct belief, but a steady course whose choices and practices remain aligned with divine guidance.

This wording introduces the way the worshippers ask to follow. A path is a course of belief and action, not only an idea to agree with. The commentary connects this request to people whose lives show obedience to Allah, making their example a guide for the person who prays.

Allah’s blessing here is guidance and the ability to live by it. The commentary associates those granted this favor with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, drawing on a Qur’anic description of them. The request is to share their faithful course, not merely to receive a title.

The prayer now marks a contrast: the worshipper asks to avoid a course that ends in divine displeasure. This is a description of a rejected path in the verse and its traditional interpretation. It should be read in its historical and religious setting, not used as a broad label for people today.

The phrase names the outcome of knowingly rejecting guidance: incurring Allah’s displeasure. The commentary records a traditional historical identification of this group with Jews among earlier religious communities. That identification concerns the interpretation’s historical setting and does not mean every Jewish person, past or present, is being judged in the same way.

The final contrast introduces another way from which the worshipper asks for protection. The wording shifts from those described through displeasure to people characterized as having lost the right way. The two descriptions help explain the prayer’s boundaries, while neither should be turned into a careless judgment about an individual.

To be astray is to have left the right course of belief and guidance. The commentary records a traditional identification with Christians in the setting of earlier religious communities. This is a historical interpretation of the verse’s wording, not a claim about every Christian or present-day community. The prayer asks Allah to keep the worshipper from error.
